title: Money Must Be Allowed In and Allowed Out
summary: Cross-border money moves through three gates: the state that lets an investment be registered, the rules that let currency be converted and sent, and the bank that agrees to carry it. A structure that ignores any gate can be perfectly legal and still unable to pay you. Design the route money will take before you commit the first dollar.
body:
A cross-border project is only as good as the route its money can travel. Before you ask what a structure earns, ask whether the money is allowed in, allowed to convert, and allowed to come home, and whether a bank will carry it every step of the way.

Recall

Q. What does a customs or investment concession usually require in return for the relief it gives?

A. Conditions: an approved project, a defined list of goods or activities, reporting, and often a commitment on investment, jobs or timing. Breach the conditions and the relief can be clawed back, so the conditions belong in your project plan, not in a drawer.

Q. State the arm's length principle in one sentence.

A. Related companies should price dealings with each other as independent parties would in comparable circumstances, so that profit lands where the real functions, assets and risks sit.

Q. Name the six lenses Omar uses to test a structure.

A. Tax, liability, banking, governance, estate and exit.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the last eight weeks taught you how a cross-border structure is taxed. This week is about something more basic: whether the money can physically move at all. A developer can hold a profitable project in a foreign country and still be unable to pay his own investors, because the investment was never registered, because the central bank will not release foreign currency, or because his bank quietly closed the account. None of those is a tax problem. Each one is a gate, and each gate has a gatekeeper with discretion.

In your grid operations work you never planned a transfer of power without checking every line, transformer and breaker on the path. Money is the same. A route is only as strong as its weakest gate, and the weakest gate is usually the one nobody mapped.

Gate one: the state lets the investment be recorded

In plain English: some countries want to know when foreign money arrives, and if you do not tell them, you may not be allowed to send it back.

The professional framing is foreign investment registration: a formal record, with a central bank, investment agency or ministry, that a non-resident has brought capital into the country. Registration can be a simple notice, a screening review that the state may refuse, or a condition of later rights such as converting profits back into foreign currency. In some countries, unregistered capital is treated as if it never arrived, so its return is not protected. The rules differ widely, change over time and are often administrative rather than statutory; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A foreign investor brings 2,000,000 dollars into a local project company as share capital. In country A, the investor files a registration within a stated period, and the central bank issues a record. Five years later, the company sells the building and wants to return 2,000,000 dollars of capital plus 1,000,000 dollars of profit. The registration is the evidence the bank needs to release foreign currency for the return. In country B, the same investor skipped the filing. The capital may still be legally owned, but the right to convert and remit it may now depend on an application, a delay and a regulator's discretion. Same project, same profit, very different exit.

Gate two: the currency may be converted and sent

In plain English: owning money in a country is not the same as being allowed to take it out in a currency you want.

The professional framing is capital controls: legal limits a state places on converting its currency or moving money across its border. They include approval requirements for remittances, caps on how much foreign currency may be bought, mandatory surrender of export earnings, waiting periods and, in a crisis, outright freezes. They are usually introduced fast, under pressure, and justified as temporary. You met their cousins in Week 43, convertibility and transfer risk. The point here is that controls are not a distant political event. They are the rules that decide whether your distribution in month 60 arrives in month 60, month 70 or never.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A project earns the equivalent of 1,000,000 dollars of profit in local currency. Under open rules, the company buys dollars at the market rate, pays any withholding tax and remits. Now suppose the central bank allows foreign currency purchases only in rationed batches of 100,000 dollars a month. The full remittance now takes ten months. If the local currency loses 10 percent against the dollar over that period, the last batches are worth less, and the average loss on the whole profit is roughly half that, about 5 percent, or 50,000 dollars, before any interest you pay on money you could not use. Nothing illegal happened. The route narrowed.

Say that out loud now.

Owning money in a country is not the same as being allowed to bring it home. I map registration, conversion and remittance before I invest.

Gate three: a bank agrees to carry it

In plain English: every dollar travels through a bank, and a bank can decline you without giving a reason.

The professional framing is know your customer (KYC): the checks a bank must run to identify its client, the people who ultimately own and control the client, the source of the money and the purpose of each transaction. Anti-money-laundering law makes the bank responsible for knowing these things, and the penalties fall on the bank. So when a structure is complex, cross-border and thinly documented, the cheapest decision for a bank is often to say no, or to close an account it already has. Banks call it de-risking. Your structure chart may be legal in every country it touches and still fail at the bank, because the bank cannot explain it to its own compliance officer in five minutes.

This is why your banking relationship is an asset you build, not a utility you assume. A bank that has seen your documents, met your people and watched clean money move through your accounts for years will process a large, unusual transfer. A bank meeting you for the first time, on the day you need it, will hold the payment and ask questions.

How the best do it

Disciplined international owners treat the route of money as a design deliverable. Before closing an investment, they produce a one-page flow-of-funds map: every entity, every bank, every currency, every registration and every approval money needs to move in and out, with who signs at each step. They keep at least two banking relationships in each important country, so one bank's decision cannot stop the business, and they send each bank a complete, current ownership pack before the bank asks. A small developer can copy all three: the map, the second bank, and the pack.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the form of each remittance, dividend, interest, fee or return of capital, decides its withholding; a capital return you cannot evidence may be taxed as income. Liability: a bank that freezes funds does not suspend your obligations to contractors and lenders. Banking: KYC readiness is a precondition of every other lens working. Governance: decide who may instruct a cross-border transfer and what evidence they must hold. Estate: executors inherit the same gates, often with fewer documents. Exit: a sale only becomes wealth when its proceeds clear all three gates.

Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed in each country on investment registration and exchange rules; a tax adviser on the form of each remittance.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming the exit route will be open because the entry route was. Entry is welcomed; exit is scrutinised. The control is to document entry as if you were already planning exit: register capital where registration protects remittance, keep the proof, and test the remittance route in a small amount early.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner wires capital informally, through a friend's account, a personal transfer, or a lender who pays a contractor directly, because it is faster. The money arrives, but the record that it was investment capital does not, and years later nobody can prove what came in.

Callback

In Week 55, Omar taught that structure is designed in sequence: flow of funds and control first, entities second. Today's three gates are what that flow of funds runs through. A chart that shows entities but not banks, currencies and approvals is half a design.

Recap

Money crossing a border passes three gates: registration with the state, permission to convert and remit, and a bank willing to carry it. Each has a gatekeeper with discretion. Map all three before you invest, and build your banking relationships before you need them.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: Argentina 2001 to 2002, when the gates closed overnight.
checklist: I have drawn a flow-of-funds map showing every entity, bank, currency and approval.
I know whether foreign capital must be registered in each country, and by when.
I hold written proof of every capital contribution and its source.
I know whether converting and remitting profit needs approval.
I hold at least two banking relationships in each important country.
Each bank has a current ownership and source-of-funds pack from me.
I have tested the remittance route with a small transfer early.
I know who may instruct a cross-border transfer, in writing.
head: Field checklist
speak: Cross-border money passes three gates. First, the state may require foreign investment to be registered, and in some countries unregistered capital loses its protected right to leave. Second, capital controls can limit converting the local currency or sending it abroad, and they arrive fast in a crisis. Third, a bank has to agree to carry the money, and under know-your-customer rules it must understand who owns my companies, where the money came from and why it is moving. A bank that cannot explain my structure will often just decline it. So before I invest, I draw a flow-of-funds map with every entity, bank, currency and approval. I register capital where registration protects its return, keep the proof, test the route with a small transfer, and hold two banks in each important country. Entry is welcomed; exit is scrutinised, so I document entry as if I were already planning the exit.
terms: Foreign investment registration — a formal record with a state body that a non-resident brought capital into the country, often a condition of later remitting it.
Capital controls — legal limits a state places on converting its currency or moving money across its border.
Know your customer (KYC) — the checks a bank must run on a client's identity, ultimate owners, source of funds and transaction purpose.

hostile.q: Your structure runs through three countries and four companies. Why should our bank take on the compliance risk of opening these accounts?
hostile.a: Because I can show you, today, every owner down to the individuals, the source of every dollar of capital with bank evidence, the purpose of each entity and each planned flow, and the registrations already filed. I am not asking you to take an unexplained risk. I am handing you the file your compliance officer would ask for, and I will update it whenever anything changes, before the transaction rather than after.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman on risk and the lender's view
title: Argentina 2001 to 2002: When the Gates Closed Overnight
summary: Argentina pegged its peso one to one to the US dollar for a decade, and people borrowed, saved and priced property as if the peg were permanent. In December 2001 the state froze bank withdrawals, and in early 2002 it ended the peg and converted dollar contracts into pesos. The lesson for a developer is that a currency promise made by a state is a policy, not a contract.
body:
For ten years Argentina promised that a peso was a dollar. People borrowed in dollars, earned in pesos and priced property as if the promise were a law of nature. When it broke, the state also closed the banks, and money that was legally yours could not be reached.

Recall

Q. In a value-added tax system, why does the timing of an input tax credit matter to a developer's cash?

A. Because tax paid on construction costs may be recoverable only months later, or only once taxable sales begin, so the project must fund that tax in the meantime. It is a working-capital cost even when the tax is eventually recovered.

Q. What usually goes wrong first when intercompany pricing fails?

A. The documentation: the price was set by habit, nobody recorded why it was arm's length, and the evidence was built after the tax authority asked.

Q. What does "sequencing" mean in structure design?

A. Doing things in the right order: decide the flow of funds and control, then form entities, then move assets and money, because reversing a step later usually costs tax or creates liability.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me because this case is about a risk that lenders and investors price and developers forget: the state itself changing the rules of money. Argentina is a large, real, well-documented example. I will keep to facts I am confident of and leave out precise figures I cannot vouch for. The story here is the pattern, and the pattern repeats wherever a currency is held up by policy.

1. Timeline

In 1991 Argentina adopted a convertibility system that fixed the peso at one to one with the US dollar and limited money creation to the country's reserves. Inflation, which had been extreme, fell. Through the 1990s dollar borrowing and dollar bank deposits became normal, and much property was priced and financed in dollars. Late in the decade the economy entered a long recession, public debt rose and confidence weakened. In December 2001, facing a run on the banks, the government imposed strict limits on cash withdrawals, a measure that became known as the corralito, the little fence. Unrest followed, and the president resigned that month. The country defaulted on much of its sovereign debt around the end of the year. In January 2002 the government abandoned convertibility, the peso was allowed to fall, and many dollar contracts and deposits were converted into pesos at rates set by the state. The peso lost most of its value against the dollar during 2002.

2. Key decisions

For a private actor, the decisive choices were made years earlier and looked prudent at the time: borrowing in dollars against peso income, keeping liquidity in local bank accounts, and signing contracts on the assumption that one peso would always buy one dollar. For the state, the decisions were to defend the peg for too long and then, when it failed, to restrict access to deposits and rewrite private contracts by decree.

3. Assumptions

Three assumptions carried the whole system. That the peg was permanent because it was written into law. That money in a bank is available on demand. That a contract in dollars stays a contract in dollars. All three proved to be policies, not facts. A law can be repealed. A bank can be ordered to stop paying. A contract can be converted by a state that decides the crisis requires it.

4. Incentives

Everyone had a reason to keep believing. Dollar loans carried lower interest rates than peso loans, so borrowers saved money each month by taking currency risk they could not see. Banks earned on dollar lending. Governments gained credibility from the peg and feared the political cost of ending it. When incentives all point the same way, the risk that nobody wants to name grows quietly.

5. Warning signs ignored

The signs were visible well before December 2001: years of recession, rising public debt, high interest rates on government borrowing that signalled lenders' doubts, and deposits leaving the banking system. For a developer, the specific warning was the currency mismatch on his own balance sheet: dollar debt, peso rent or peso buyers, and peso cash. Roman's point is simple. If your income and your debt are in different currencies, you are running a currency position whether you meant to or not.

Say that out loud now.

A currency promise made by a state is a policy, not a contract, and it can be withdrawn on a weekend.

6. Point of no return

For a private borrower, the point of no return was the moment liquidity sat behind the fence. Once withdrawals were limited, a developer could not move cash to a safer bank, a safer currency or a safer country. Every option that would have helped required money he could no longer reach. The planning window closed before the crisis, not during it.

A hypothetical example of the arithmetic, using round numbers. A developer owes 10,000,000 dollars and expects sales worth 15,000,000 dollars in local currency at a one to one rate. If the local currency falls to three per dollar and prices adjust only partly, say to 25,000,000 local units, his sales are now worth about 8,300,000 dollars. A project with 5,000,000 dollars of margin now owes 1,700,000 dollars more than it can raise. The building did not change. The currency did. In the real crisis, state conversion of contracts changed which side bore that loss; the outcome for any particular party depended on decrees, courts and later settlements, which is exactly why no developer could plan around it.

7. Root cause

The root cause, for anyone exposed, was treating the convertibility of money as a fixed property of the country rather than as a risk to be priced and limited. The peg made the risk look like zero. Zero-looking risks are not managed, so when they arrive they arrive in full.

The prevention rule

Rule 63: Never let my ability to pay depend on a currency promise or a bank access I do not control; match debt to the currency of income, keep reserves outside the system I am exposed to, and decide in advance the trigger that makes me move money.

What a developer would have done differently

Ford's reading for a developer in that market is practical. Borrow in the currency the buyers pay in, even at a higher interest rate, because the higher rate is a visible cost and the mismatch is an invisible one. Keep the reserve that pays the next six months of interest outside the country's banking system. And price sales contracts so that the currency risk is shared or stated, rather than assumed away. None of this would have made the crisis painless. It would have kept a developer solvent long enough to finish and sell.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that a long period of stability teaches you the gate cannot close. The control is a written trigger: a list of observable signals, such as reserves falling, withdrawal limits proposed, or a widening gap between official and market exchange rates, that obliges you to act before the fence goes up. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer and a tax adviser in each country before you move reserves across a border.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads country risk as a reason not to invest at all, or as nothing. Neither is right. The mature response is to invest with a currency plan: matched debt, reserves held elsewhere, and a trigger written down while you are calm.

Callback

In Week 43, Roman taught convertibility risk and transfer risk as separate items on a country-risk register. Argentina shows them arriving together, with a third, contract conversion, on top. In Week 2, the pre-mortem asked you to imagine the project dead and explain why. "The money was there but we could not reach it" belongs on every cross-border pre-mortem.

Recap

Argentina pegged the peso to the dollar for a decade; in December 2001 withdrawals were restricted, and in early 2002 the peg ended and contracts were converted. The root cause, for exposed parties, was treating a policy as a fact. Rule 63: never let my ability to pay depend on a currency promise or a bank access I do not control.

Next: Nadia on The Money: what it really costs to move money across a border.
checklist: I list every currency my income, debt and costs are in.
I name any currency mismatch on my balance sheet in writing.
I match project debt to the currency of project income where I can.
I hold part of my reserves outside the banking system I am exposed to.
I keep a written list of warning signals for capital controls.
I have decided in advance which signal makes me act.
I have taken legal and tax advice before moving any reserves.
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 63: Never let my ability to pay depend on a currency promise or a bank access I do not control; match debt to the currency of income, keep reserves outside the system I am exposed to, and decide in advance the trigger that makes me move money.
speak: Argentina fixed its peso at one to one with the US dollar in 1991. For a decade people borrowed in dollars, earned in pesos and priced property as if the peg were permanent. In December 2001, facing a bank run, the state limited cash withdrawals, the corralito. In January 2002 it ended the peg, the peso fell, and many dollar contracts were converted into pesos by the state. The lesson is that a currency promise made by a state is a policy, not a contract. Anyone with dollar debt and peso income was running a currency position without admitting it, and once cash was behind the fence, every escape required money they could not reach. My rule is Rule 63: never let my ability to pay depend on a currency promise or bank access I do not control. I match debt to the currency of income, keep reserves outside the system I am exposed to, and write down in advance the warning signal that makes me move.
terms: Currency peg — a policy fixing one currency's exchange rate to another, held up by the state's reserves and willingness.
Corralito — the popular name for the limits on bank withdrawals Argentina imposed in December 2001.
Currency mismatch — earning in one currency while owing in another, so exchange-rate moves change your ability to pay.

hostile.q: Your rent is in local currency and your loan is in dollars. What happens to your coverage if the currency loses a third of its value?
hostile.a: Coverage falls by roughly a third in dollar terms, which in my downside case breaches the covenant. That is why I am not proposing this structure as it stands. I want either local-currency debt for a meaningful part of the loan, leases indexed or priced in dollars where the market allows, or a reserve and hedge sized to carry the shortfall, and I will show you the case at that devaluation before you commit.

title: What Moving Money Really Costs
summary: Every cross-border transfer loses value in three places: the exchange spread, the bank charges, and the time money spends waiting. Over a project's life those small losses compound into a real cut to the investor's return. Count them, put them in the pro forma, and choose routes that shrink them.
body:
Money that crosses a border arrives smaller and later than it left. The spread, the fees and the waiting time are real costs, and a pro forma that ignores them overstates the return you can actually spend.

Recall

Q. In a negotiation over an investment concession, what is usually worth more than the headline relief?

A. The conditions and their stability: how long the relief lasts, what triggers clawback, and whether a change in law can withdraw it. A smaller, certain concession can beat a larger, fragile one.

Q. How does an intercompany fee move profit between countries?

A. It is a cost to the payer and income to the receiver, so it shifts taxable profit from one country to the other. That is exactly why it must be priced at arm's length and supported by evidence of a real service.

Q. In structure design, why do we draw the flow of funds before the entities?

A. Because entities exist to carry money and control. If you know how money must move, in and out, you can choose entities that make that movement cheap and lawful, instead of forcing money through boxes chosen first.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer who works across Canada and Guyana will move money across a border many times: capital in, construction payments, imported materials, loan service, and finally profit out. Each transfer leaks a little. Individually the leaks look trivial. Added across a project they can equal a meaningful fraction of the developer's own profit. Investors and lenders do not see this leakage unless you show them, and you will not see it unless you count it.

The three leaks

In plain English: you pay to change money, you pay to send it, and you lose value while it waits.

The professional framing names three costs. First, the exchange spread: the difference between the rate at which a bank buys a currency and the rate at which it sells it. You see a mid-market rate on a screen; you transact at a worse one, and the difference is the bank's margin. Second, transaction charges: sending fees, intermediary bank fees deducted along the way, and receiving fees. Third, the cost of delay: money in transit or waiting for an approval earns nothing, and if the currency moves against you meanwhile, you lose value as well. Spreads and fees are commercial terms negotiated with banks, not regulated rates; they vary by bank, currency, size and relationship.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. You convert 1,000,000 dollars into local currency to fund construction. The bank's rate is 2 percent worse than mid-market, so you lose 20,000 dollars of value on the spread. Sending and intermediary fees cost another 500 dollars. The funds take five business days to clear. On that one transfer you lose about 20,500 dollars, a little over 2 percent. Now repeat in reverse when profit comes home: another 2 percent. A round trip on the same capital costs about 4 percent before any tax.

How the leakage reaches the return

In plain English: the leaks are small per transfer, but they fall on equity, and equity is the thinnest slice.

The professional framing is that conversion costs are borne by the investor's capital, so they reduce the equity multiple and the internal rate of return (IRR), the annual rate at which the investment's cash flows break even. Because equity is usually a fraction of the project cost, a cost measured against the whole capital flow is a much larger cut to the equity return.

A second worked example, hypothetical. An investor puts in 3,000,000 dollars and expects 4,500,000 dollars back after five years, an equity multiple of 1.5. Converting in at 2 percent costs 60,000 dollars, so only 2,940,000 dollars reaches the project. Suppose the project still grows that to the same proportional result, about 4,410,000 dollars. Converting out at 2 percent costs about 88,000 dollars, leaving about 4,322,000 dollars. The multiple falls from 1.5 to about 1.44. Add a ten-month remittance delay with a 5 percent average currency loss on the profit, as we saw in Day 1, and the multiple slips further. None of this shows up in a pro forma that models one currency at one rate on one date.

Say that out loud now.

Every border crossing costs spread, fees and time, and those costs fall on equity, the thinnest slice.

Shrinking the leaks

The controls are practical. Negotiate the spread in writing before a large conversion; banks price relationships, and a quoted rate on a named amount is a commitment you can compare. Convert in fewer, larger amounts where the rules allow, rather than many small ones. Hold a working balance in the currency you spend, so you are not converting under pressure. Match currencies: pay foreign suppliers from foreign income where you can, instead of converting both ways. And model leakage explicitly in the pro forma, as its own line, so that the investor return you quote is the return they will actually receive.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's point for your personal balance sheet: wealth held in a currency you will not spend carries a hidden discount, the cost of converting it when you need it, and a hidden risk, the chance that the gate narrows first. Record personal assets in the currency of your future spending, show the conversion cost and the access route beside each line, and keep part of your liquidity floor in that spending currency. That is a planning principle, not product advice; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Ethics and anti-corruption

This month's thread. Where money is slow, someone will offer to make it fast: an official who can expedite an approval, a fixer at a bank, a contact who knows a cheaper rate off the books. Every one of those offers turns a cost problem into a criminal and reputational one, and in many countries both the payer and the person who arranged it can be liable [unverified — confirm independently].

Your rule is simple and must be decided now, not in the moment. Delay is a cost you price. A payment to speed a public official's duty is not an option you consider. Write that in your company's policy, tell every adviser and agent, and record any approach in writing the day it happens.

A leakage line in practice

A simple way to model it: add a row under each capital inflow and each distribution called conversion and transfer cost, set it at your negotiated spread plus a fixed fee per transfer, and add a third row for delay, with an assumed number of days and an assumed monthly currency drift. Then run the downside with the spread doubled and the delay tripled. If the investor's return still clears its hurdle, the route is robust. If it does not, the currency plan needs work before the money moves, not after.

Show the investor both rows. A sponsor who volunteers the leakage line is trusted with the rest of the model. A sponsor whose investor finds it at exit is not trusted with the next deal.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is quoting investors a return in one currency while the project lives in another, so the leakage arrives as a surprise at exit. The control is a currency line in the pro forma and a return quoted after conversion, at a stated assumed rate and spread.

The beginner's mistake

Using the screen rate in the model. The screen rate is the price nobody pays.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage warned that after-tax leakage turns an attractive gross IRR into an ordinary net one. Currency and transfer leakage is the same idea one layer down: count every cost between the building's cash and the investor's pocket, or the number you quote is not real.

Recap

Each transfer loses value to the spread, the fees and the wait. Those costs fall on equity, so a few percent of capital becomes a larger cut to the equity return. Negotiate spreads, convert less often, hold working currency, match currencies and model the leakage as its own line.

Next: Omar on The Rules: what the law requires before money may move.
checklist: My pro forma shows currency conversion cost as its own line.
I quote investor returns after conversion, at a stated rate and spread.
I obtain a written quote for any large conversion before I instruct it.
I convert in fewer, larger amounts where the rules allow.
I hold a working balance in the currency I spend.
I pay foreign costs from foreign income where I can.
My company policy forbids payments to speed an official's duty.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every time money crosses a border it loses value in three places. The exchange spread, the gap between the rate I see on screen and the rate the bank gives me. The fees, including intermediary banks that deduct charges on the way. And time, because money waiting for clearance or approval earns nothing and can lose value if the currency moves. On a hypothetical one million dollar conversion, a 2 percent spread costs twenty thousand dollars, and a round trip in and out costs about 4 percent before tax. Those costs fall on equity, the thinnest slice, so they cut the equity multiple and the IRR more than they seem to. So I negotiate spreads in writing, convert in fewer larger amounts, hold a working balance in the currency I spend, match currencies where I can, and show conversion as its own line in the pro forma, so the return I quote is the return investors actually receive.
terms: Exchange spread — the difference between a bank's buying and selling rates for a currency, which is its margin on a conversion.
Mid-market rate — the midpoint between buying and selling rates, the rate shown on screens and paid by nobody.
Equity multiple — total cash returned to investors divided by total cash they put in.

hostile.q: Your pro forma shows a 1.5 times equity multiple. Is that what lands in my account in my own currency?
hostile.a: No, and I have shown you the difference. The 1.5 is the project result. After an assumed conversion spread in and out and a remittance delay in my downside case, the multiple in your currency is about 1.44, and lower if the currency weakens. I quote you that net figure as the headline, with the assumed rate and spread stated, and I have a working-currency policy designed to keep the leakage near that estimate.

title: The Rules Money Moves Under
summary: Three bodies of rules govern cross-border money: investment screening and registration, exchange and capital-movement rules, and anti-money-laundering law with its beneficial-ownership duties. Each is set by statute, regulation or central-bank directive, and each can change quickly. Know which apply, who enforces them, and what evidence they demand.
body:
Moving money is regulated by three separate systems that rarely talk to each other: the rules on foreign investment, the rules on currency and capital movement, and the rules against money laundering. Satisfying one does not satisfy the others.

Recall

Q. Name three things a checkpoint on indirect tax should be able to explain without notes.

A. How input tax credits work and when they are recoverable; how customs value and duty are determined on imported goods; and what an investment concession requires in return for its relief.

Q. What is transfer-pricing documentation for?

A. To show, with evidence written at the time, that intercompany prices were set at arm's length: the functions, assets and risks of each party, the method chosen and the comparables used.

Q. In structure design, what does "control" mean on a flow-of-funds chart?

A. Who has the legal and practical power to decide: who appoints directors, who signs, who can move money. It is drawn alongside ownership because the two often differ.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the rules in this lesson are mostly administrative and fast-moving. They live in regulations, central-bank directives and agency guidance, not in a single statute you can read once. That makes them easy to miss and costly to break. A missed filing can turn a lawful investment into one that cannot be repatriated. A missed beneficial-ownership update can freeze an account. This lesson gives you the map; the detail comes from licensed counsel in each country.

System one: foreign investment rules

In plain English: the state decides whether it wants your money, and on what terms.

The professional framing is investment screening and registration. Many countries review foreign acquisitions of land or businesses above a threshold, in sensitive sectors, or on national-security grounds. Some restrict foreign ownership of residential property or land outright. Some require registration of foreign capital, and tie protected rights, such as remitting profit, to that registration. Others offer incentives through an investment agency in exchange for conditions. The key questions are always the same: is approval required before closing, or only notice after; who decides; what can they impose; and what happens if you close first.

A worked example, hypothetical. A non-resident buyer signs to acquire a residential development site. In one country the purchase needs no approval. In a second, the state restricts non-resident purchases of certain residential property, subject to exceptions. In a third, the acquisition is allowed but the capital must be registered within a stated period to protect later remittance. The same contract creates three different risk profiles, and the purchase agreement should make closing conditional on the approval or registration that actually applies.

System two: exchange and capital-movement rules

In plain English: the central bank decides whether, and how fast, the local currency can be turned into another one and sent away.

The professional framing is exchange control. Where it exists, it can require approval for outward payments, limit foreign-currency accounts, require reporting of transfers, or ration foreign currency. Where it does not exist in law, the market can still ration it in practice: commercial banks may simply not have enough foreign currency to sell at the quoted rate, and payments queue. Treat legal controls and practical scarcity as two different risks; the first is in the regulations, the second shows up only in banking experience.

System three: anti-money-laundering and beneficial ownership

In plain English: every bank, lawyer and in many places real estate agent must know who really owns you and where your money came from, and must report what looks wrong.

The professional framing has two parts. First, beneficial ownership: the natural persons who ultimately own or control an entity, as distinct from the companies or nominees on the register. Many countries now require companies to keep, and sometimes file, a register of these individuals [unverified — confirm independently]. Second, suspicious transaction reporting: the duty of regulated institutions to report transactions they suspect involve criminal proceeds, usually without telling the customer. That second duty is why a bank may freeze or decline without explanation. It is not hiding a reason from you to be difficult; the law may forbid it from telling you.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Your project company receives 500,000 dollars from a new co-investor's holding company in a third country. The bank asks for the holding company's ownership down to the individuals and evidence of where the 500,000 dollars came from. You do not have it, because you assumed the co-investor's bank had checked. The funds are held. Construction payments due the next week are late. The fix is not to argue with the bank. It is to collect, before signing any investment, the same beneficial-ownership and source-of-funds evidence the bank will need, and to pass it to the bank before the money arrives.

Say that out loud now.

Three rulebooks, three regulators: investment, exchange, and anti-money-laundering. Passing one does not pass the others.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source in both countries. Canada generally does not impose exchange controls on converting or remitting money, but it screens certain foreign investments under federal law and has, in recent years, restricted some purchases of residential property by non-Canadians, subject to exceptions [unverified — confirm independently]. Its anti-money-laundering regime places reporting duties on banks and on other regulated sectors, including some real estate participants, and is supervised by a federal financial intelligence unit [unverified — confirm independently].

Guyana has an investment promotion agency that facilitates foreign investment and administers incentives, and an anti-money-laundering law that places customer-due-diligence and reporting duties on financial institutions and designated businesses [unverified — confirm independently]. How readily foreign currency can be bought and remitted in practice can depend on bank liquidity at the time, which is a banking question as much as a legal one [unverified — confirm independently]. The habit is the same in both: identify the rule, the regulator and the evidence before closing, and verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed in each country on investment, exchange and anti-money-laundering obligations.

Who enforces, and what they can do

Each rulebook has its own enforcer with different powers. An investment agency or ministry can refuse, impose conditions, or require divestment after the fact. A central bank can refuse approval, delay conversion, or fine. A financial intelligence unit receives reports, shares them with law enforcement and supervises the institutions that report. The bank itself enforces anti-money-laundering rules on you by declining, holding or exiting. Of the four, the bank acts fastest and explains least, which is why your evidence pack is built for the bank first.

The practical habit is a rules register: one row per country and rulebook, with the rule, the regulator, the trigger, the deadline, the evidence required and who on your team owns it. Review it at every closing and every change of ownership.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is closing a transaction before the applicable approval, registration or bank due diligence is complete, so the money arrives into a structure that is lawful but frozen. The control is to make each applicable approval a condition precedent in the contract and to deliver the bank's due-diligence pack before funds are sent.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the bank's questions as an insult and the regulator's forms as paperwork. Both are the price of being able to move money later. Answer fully, early, and in writing.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught how to instruct professionals: a precise question, a stated scope, a written answer. Today's three systems are three separate questions, often for three separate specialists. An instruction that asks only "is this structure legal" will not tell you whether the money can come home.

Recap

Investment rules decide whether the state accepts your money and on what terms. Exchange rules, and practical scarcity, decide whether it can be converted and sent. Anti-money-laundering law decides what every bank must know about you, and lets it act without explaining. Make each a condition of closing.

Next: Roman on The Numbers: pricing a remittance route step by step.
checklist: I have listed the investment, exchange and anti-money-laundering rules in each country.
I know whether each investment needs approval before closing or notice after.
Each required approval or registration is a condition precedent in the contract.
I hold beneficial-ownership evidence for every co-investor down to the individuals.
I hold source-of-funds evidence before any investor's money is sent.
I deliver the bank's due-diligence pack before funds arrive.
I keep my company's beneficial-ownership register current.
I have instructed counsel in each country with a written scope.
head: Field checklist
speak: Cross-border money is governed by three separate rulebooks. Investment rules decide whether a state accepts foreign capital and on what terms: screening, ownership limits, registration and incentives. Exchange rules decide whether the local currency can be converted and sent, and even where the law is open, banks can ration foreign currency in practice. Anti-money-laundering law requires banks and other regulated firms to identify my beneficial owners, the real individuals behind my companies, check the source of my funds, and report suspicious transactions, sometimes without telling me. Passing one rulebook does not pass the others. So I make each required approval or registration a condition of closing, I collect beneficial-ownership and source-of-funds evidence from every co-investor before money moves, and I hand the bank its due-diligence pack before the funds arrive. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed in each country.
terms: Beneficial ownership — the natural persons who ultimately own or control an entity, as distinct from the names on its register.
Suspicious transaction reporting — a regulated firm's duty to report transactions it suspects involve criminal proceeds, usually without telling the customer.
Exchange control — legal rules on converting a currency and moving money across a country's border.

hostile.q: Your co-investor's money comes through a holding company in a third country. Who are the individuals behind it, and how do you know the money is clean?
hostile.a: The individuals are named in the ownership chart in your pack, down to each natural person with a meaningful interest, with identity documents. Source of funds is evidenced by bank statements and the sale documents that generated the money. I collected that before signing, and our investment agreement lets me refuse or return funds if any of it changes or proves false.

title: Pricing a Remittance Route, Step by Step
summary: A worked calculation takes hypothetical project profit from a foreign project company to an investor's home account, through tax, conversion, fees and delay. Then the same calculation is run under a capital-control scenario. The gap between the two is what a currency plan is worth.
body:
A remittance route can be priced like any other cost. Take the profit, subtract each leak in order, and read off what arrives. Then run it again with the gate narrowed, and you know what your currency plan has to protect.

Recall

Q. What are the three gates cross-border money must pass?

A. The state's investment registration, the exchange rules that let currency be converted and sent, and a bank willing to carry the money under its know-your-customer duties.

Q. Why is a transfer-pricing number not enough on its own?

A. Because the authority tests the evidence behind it: a price that is reasonable but undocumented can be adjusted, while a documented analysis of functions, assets, risks and comparables can be defended.

Q. What is "leakage" in structure design?

A. Every cost between the project's cash and the investor's pocket: entity-level tax, withholding on distributions, conversion and banking costs, and administration.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, investors ask one question at the end of every deal: how much reached me, and when. A developer who can answer that with a step-by-step calculation, including what happens if a currency gate narrows, is a developer they trust with cross-border money. Today's numbers are hypothetical and round. The tax rate is an assumption for teaching, not a statement of any country's law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Step 1: the base route

A foreign project company has distributable profit equal to 2,000,000 dollars, held in local currency at an exchange rate of 200 local units per dollar. So it holds 400,000,000 local units.

Assume a dividend withholding tax of 10 percent. Withholding is 40,000,000 units, leaving 360,000,000 units to convert.

The bank's selling rate for dollars is 2 percent worse than the mid-market rate of 200, so the rate is 204 units per dollar. 360,000,000 divided by 204 is about 1,764,700 dollars.

Outgoing, intermediary and receiving fees total 300 dollars. Net arrival: about 1,764,400 dollars.

So 2,000,000 dollars of profit at the mid-market rate becomes about 1,764,400 dollars in the investor's account, a total leakage of about 235,600 dollars, or 11.8 percent. Of that, 10 points are tax and about 1.8 points are conversion and fees. The tax is a policy question for Elias. The conversion leak is a commercial one you can negotiate.

Say that out loud now.

Profit, less withholding, converted at the real rate, less fees, equals what arrives. Then I run it with the gate narrowed.

Step 2: the narrowed gate

Now assume the central bank introduces rationing: the company may buy only the equivalent of 200,000 dollars a month. Assume, too, that the local currency weakens steadily by 1 percent a month against the dollar while you wait.

The 360,000,000 units after tax now take about nine months to convert. In month 1 the rate is about 204; by month 9 it is about 204 multiplied by 1.01 to the eighth power, roughly 221. The average rate across the nine months is about 212.

360,000,000 divided by 212 is about 1,698,100 dollars. Fees on nine transfers instead of one: about 2,700 dollars. Net arrival: about 1,695,400 dollars, and it arrives over nine months rather than at once.

The narrowing costs about 69,000 dollars of value, plus the time value of waiting. If the investor's money is worth 8 percent a year to them, receiving the average dollar about four months late costs roughly another 2.7 percent of the amount, about 45,000 dollars. Total cost of the narrowed gate: roughly 114,000 dollars on a 2,000,000 dollar profit.

Step 3: what the cost buys you as a plan

Now price the controls. If you had distributed profit quarterly as earned instead of holding it to the end, much of the cash would have left before rationing began. If you had held the project's working reserve in dollars, offshore, the investor could be paid from the reserve while the local currency waited to convert. If you had local-currency costs still to pay, you could use the trapped units to pay them rather than converting at all.

A second worked example of that last control, hypothetical. The company still owes 100,000,000 units to a local contractor and has a dollar reserve of 500,000 dollars offshore. Instead of converting trapped profit, it pays the contractor from the trapped units and releases 500,000 dollars of the offshore reserve to investors now. The conversion queue shrinks by 100,000,000 units, about five months of rationing at the rationed amount, and investors receive cash today. No rule was bent. The currencies were matched.

Reading the result

Present the two routes side by side: base arrival about 1,764,400 dollars at once; narrowed arrival about 1,695,400 dollars over nine months, worth roughly 1,650,000 dollars in today's money. The difference, about 114,000 dollars, is the value at risk from the gate. That number justifies the cost of an offshore reserve, a second bank, or a distribution policy that sends money out as it is earned. It also tells a lender how much cushion the investor-level cash flow really has.

A worked check on the arithmetic

Check the narrowed-gate figures the way a lender's analyst would. 360,000,000 units at 200,000 dollars a month at a rate near 204 is about 40,800,000 units a month, so about nine months to clear: correct. The rate path runs from 204 to about 221, a little over 8 percent of drift across eight steps, so an average near 212 is reasonable. 360,000,000 divided by 212 is about 1,698,100: correct. The point of the check is not precision. It is that every number traces to a stated assumption, so anyone can change one assumption and see what moves.

Now run a severe case for the investment committee. Double the monthly depreciation to 2 percent and halve the monthly allowance to 100,000 dollars. The queue now takes about eighteen months, and the average rate drifts toward roughly 240. 360,000,000 divided by 240 is about 1,500,000 dollars, arriving across a year and a half. In today's money at 8 percent, that is worth roughly 1,410,000 dollars. The severe case cuts the investor's realised profit by nearly a third against the base route. That is the number that decides whether an offshore reserve is optional or required.

Turning the result into a policy

Translate the cases into three written policy lines. First, a distribution policy: profit above an agreed working balance is distributed each quarter, so it does not accumulate behind the gate. Second, a reserve policy: a stated number of months of investor distributions and debt service is held in the investor's currency outside the project's country. Third, a trigger policy: named signals, such as a new rationing rule or a widening gap between the official and market rates, accelerate distributions. Each line costs something in normal times. Each is priced by today's calculation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is presenting the base route as the only route. A single-route calculation looks precise and hides the scenario that matters. The control is always to show the narrowed-gate case beside it, with the assumptions stated.

The beginner's mistake

Converting at the mid-market rate and forgetting fees, then treating the tax rate as the only leak. The conversion leak is smaller than tax, but it is the one you control.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman built stress tests with a base, a downside and a severe case, and asked what single variable breaks the deal. Today's narrowed gate is that discipline applied to the investor's cash, not the project's: the building can be performing perfectly while the investor's return breaks at the border.

Recap

Price the route in order: profit, withholding, real conversion rate, fees, arrival. Then narrow the gate with rationing and devaluation, and value the delay. The gap is what a currency plan must protect, and it justifies reserves, second banks and earlier distributions.

Next: REGA on The Room: the bank onboarding meeting.
checklist: I price every remittance route in order: profit, tax, conversion, fees, arrival.
I use the bank's real rate, not the mid-market rate.
I always show a narrowed-gate case beside the base case.
I value delay at the investor's cost of money.
I consider distributing profit as earned rather than at the end.
I hold part of the working reserve in the investor's currency.
I use trapped local currency to pay local costs where I can.
head: Field checklist
speak: I price a remittance route the way I price any cost. Hypothetically, start with two million dollars of profit held in local currency. Take off dividend withholding at an assumed 10 percent. Convert at the bank's real rate, about 2 percent worse than the screen. Take off fees. About 1.76 million dollars arrives, a leakage near 12 percent, of which roughly two points are conversion I can negotiate. Then I narrow the gate: the central bank rations dollars to two hundred thousand a month and the currency weakens 1 percent a month. Now about 1.70 million arrives over nine months, worth roughly 1.65 million today. The gap, about one hundred and fourteen thousand dollars, is the value at risk at the border. That justifies an offshore dollar reserve, a second bank, paying local costs with trapped local currency, and distributing profit as it is earned rather than holding it to the end.
terms: Withholding tax — tax deducted at source by the payer on a cross-border payment such as a dividend, interest or fee.
Rationing — a limit, set by a central bank or by bank scarcity, on how much foreign currency can be bought in a period.
Time value of money — the principle that a dollar received later is worth less than a dollar received today.

hostile.q: Your investor return assumes profit converts at today's rate on the day of sale. What if the central bank rations dollars?
hostile.a: Then the return falls, and I have shown by how much. In my narrowed-gate case, nine months of rationing and a steady 1 percent monthly depreciation cost about 114,000 dollars on 2,000,000 of profit, including delay. My plan reduces that: quarterly distributions as profit is earned, a dollar reserve held offshore, and paying local costs from local currency so less needs converting.

title: The Bank Onboarding Meeting
summary: A composite scene: opening project accounts with a new bank for a cross-border structure. The relationship manager wants the deal; the compliance officer has to be satisfied. Learn the lines to say, the lines never to say, and the real question behind every document request.
body:
In a bank onboarding meeting you are not selling the project. You are making it easy for a compliance officer to say yes and defend that yes later. Bring the file before they ask, answer completely, and never treat a question as an accusation.

Recall

Q. In the remittance calculation, what is the value at risk from a narrowed gate?

A. The difference between what arrives on the base route and what arrives, in today's money, under rationing and devaluation. It tells you what a currency plan must protect.

Q. In a transfer-pricing review meeting, what should you never do?

A. Create documents after the fact and present them as contemporaneous, or speculate about a price you cannot support. Say what was done, show what exists, and confirm the rest in writing.

Q. In a structure-design meeting, what does a good first slide show?

A. The flow of funds and control on one page: who owns what, who decides, where money comes in and where it leaves.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, your bank can stop your project faster than your lender, your regulator or your contractor. It can do it lawfully, without a hearing and sometimes without a reason. The way to prevent that is not argument after the event. It is the onboarding meeting, done so well that the bank understands you better than most of its clients.

The setup

This is a composite scene with hypothetical facts. You want to open accounts for a new project company that will receive investor capital from abroad, pay local contractors and later remit profit. The structure has a holding company in one country, the project company in another, and two co-investors with their own holding companies. Across the table: Lena, the relationship manager, who wants the business, and Theo, from compliance, who joined at the last minute and has your ownership chart in front of him with three entities circled.

The opening

Say: "Thank you for taking the time. I have brought the full file so you do not have to chase it. It shows every owner down to the individuals, the source of every dollar of capital, the purpose of each company, and the payments we expect over the next eighteen months. I would rather you ask hard questions now than hold a payment later."

That last sentence tells Theo you understand his job. It costs you nothing and moves him from gatekeeper to collaborator.

Say that out loud now.

The question behind the question

Theo asks: "Why is there a holding company in a third country?" The question behind it is: "Is this layer here to hide someone or something?" Answer the real question. Say: "It holds the interest of two investors who are not resident here, and it is where their own advisers want the investment held. Here are its registers and the individuals behind it. It has no other activity, and it does not hold anything I have not shown you." If the honest answer is a tax reason, say so plainly, and show that the tax position has been advised.

Theo asks: "Where did the 2,000,000 dollars of initial capital come from?" The question behind it is: "Can I trace it to a lawful source with documents?" Answer with documents, not adjectives: "From the sale of a property in 2025, hypothetical example; here is the sale agreement, the settlement statement and the bank statement showing the proceeds arriving." Never answer "It is clean, you can trust me." The bank is not permitted to rely on trust.

Lena asks: "What volume of transactions should we expect?" The question behind it is: "Will your activity match what you tell us, so our monitoring does not flag it?" Give a realistic schedule, then promise to update it. Unexpected activity that contradicts your stated profile is one of the commonest reasons an account is reviewed.

The lines never to say

Never say "Can we keep this simple and skip the beneficial-owner details?" That sentence alone can end the relationship. Never say "My other bank did not need this." It invites the reply that your other bank may soon need it too. Never suggest splitting a large deposit into smaller ones; breaking transactions up to avoid reporting is itself an offence in many countries [unverified — confirm independently], and even the suggestion will be recorded. And never ask whether a transaction "will be reported." The bank cannot discuss its reporting with you, and asking makes you look like someone with a reason to worry.

When to stay silent

When Theo is reading a document, stop talking. Filling the silence with explanations sounds like nerves and invites new questions. When he asks something you do not know, do not guess. Say: "I don't know. I'll confirm in writing by Friday," and then do it. A wrong answer on source of funds is far worse than a late one.

Holding your state

The questions can feel personal, as if your honesty is on trial. Reframe them before the meeting: these are the same questions the bank must ask everyone, and each complete answer makes the next transfer easier. If you feel your pulse climb, slow your speech and drop your pitch slightly. That is a practitioner habit, not a law of physiology, but it reliably steadies most people.

The close

Say: "What else would your compliance team need to be comfortable, today or at our first large transfer?" Write the list. Then agree a contact for unusual payments, so a large exit remittance in two years is announced to someone who remembers you, not discovered by a system that does not.

A second scene: the account review two years later

Fast-forward, still composite. The building is sold and you want to remit 3,000,000 dollars of profit in one transfer. A new compliance analyst, who has never met you, holds the payment and asks for the sale agreement, the settlement statement, the tax clearance and the ownership chart as it stands today. If your standing pack is current, you send it within the hour and the payment moves within days. If the co-investor changed his holding company last year and nobody told the bank, you now have a mismatch between the file and reality, and the payment waits while it is resolved.

Say: "Thank you for flagging it. Attached are the sale documents, the tax clearance and our current ownership chart, which matches the update we sent in March." That sentence is only possible if the March update was sent. The meeting two years later is won or lost in the months between.

Do not escalate over the analyst's head on the first day. Ask what is outstanding, supply it, and only then ask your named contact to help. Pressure on compliance reads as a reason for more scrutiny.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating onboarding as a one-time hurdle. Banks review relationships periodically, and changes in ownership, activity or country trigger fresh checks. The control is a standing ownership and source-of-funds pack, updated whenever anything changes and sent to the bank before it asks.

The beginner's mistake

Arriving with the relationship manager's enthusiasm and no file, assuming the deal's quality will carry the compliance review. Compliance does not score the deal. It scores the evidence.

Callback

In Week 6, you learned to handle a hostile question in three moves: acknowledge, bridge, answer, and to say "I'll confirm by Friday" rather than guess. The onboarding meeting is that drill with real consequences. And Week 4's slow breathing belongs before the meeting, in the car park with the engine off, never while driving.

Recap

Bring the complete file before you are asked. Answer the question behind the question with documents. Never ask to skip ownership detail, split deposits or know what is reported. Stay silent while documents are read, confirm unknowns in writing, and agree a contact for unusual payments.

Next: Kema on the week's review: registration, controls, KYC and banking relationships.
checklist: I bring a complete ownership and source-of-funds file to onboarding.
I can explain the purpose of every entity in one sentence.
I evidence the source of capital with documents, not assurances.
I give the bank a realistic transaction profile and update it.
I never ask to skip ownership detail or split a deposit.
I confirm unknown answers in writing by a stated date.
I have a named bank contact for unusual payments.
head: Field checklist
speak: In a bank onboarding meeting I am not selling the project; I am making it easy for compliance to say yes and defend it later. I bring the full file before I am asked: every owner down to the individuals, the source of every dollar of capital with documents, the purpose of each company, and the payments I expect. When compliance asks why a holding company exists, the real question is whether it hides something, so I answer that directly with its registers and owners. When they ask about source of funds, I answer with sale agreements and bank statements, never with 'trust me'. I never ask to skip beneficial-owner details, never suggest splitting a deposit, and never ask whether something will be reported. When they read, I stay silent. When I do not know, I say I will confirm in writing by Friday. And I agree a named contact for large unusual payments, so my exit remittance is expected, not flagged.
terms: Relationship manager — the bank officer responsible for winning and serving a client, who does not make the compliance decision.
Transaction profile — the expected size, frequency and type of a client's transactions, which the bank monitors against actual activity.
De-risking — a bank's decision to decline or exit clients it judges too costly or risky to monitor.

hostile.q: Your chart has an entity in a third country with no employees. Why shouldn't we treat that as a red flag?
hostile.a: You should ask about it, and here is the answer. It holds the interest of two non-resident investors and has no other activity. Here are its registers, its directors, the individuals who own it, and the advice on why it is held there. If anything about it changes, ownership, activity or country, you will hear from me before the change, not after it.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 63 Review: Registration, Controls, KYC and Banks
summary: Six questions test the week: the three gates, Argentina's lesson, the cost of moving money, the three rulebooks and the bank meeting. A Red Pen drill finds the defects in a hypothetical funding memo, and a boardroom drill explains the week in two minutes.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: money you own abroad is only wealth when it can be registered, converted, carried by a bank and brought home, so you design that route before you invest, not after.

Recall

Q. What is the exchange spread?

A. The difference between a bank's buying and selling rates for a currency; the bank's margin on a conversion, and a cost you can negotiate.

Q. What is an intercompany service agreement for?

A. To record, before the service is provided, what is being supplied, by whom, at what price and on what basis, so that the fee can be shown to be real and at arm's length.

Q. What is the purpose of a structure's governance lens?

A. To test who decides, who signs and how authority is recorded, so that the structure works in practice and is not only drawn on paper.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the tax weeks of this phase are wasted if the money cannot move. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the three gates money must pass to cross a border?

Answer: Registration with the state where required, permission to convert and remit under exchange rules or in practice, and a bank willing to carry the money under its know-your-customer duties.

Question 2. Why can unregistered foreign capital be a problem at exit?

Answer: Because in some countries the protected right to convert and remit capital and profit depends on registration at entry. Without it, return can depend on an application and a regulator's discretion, and a capital return you cannot evidence may be taxed as income.

Question 3. What was the root cause of losses for those exposed in Argentina 2001 to 2002?

Answer: Treating a currency peg and access to bank deposits as fixed facts rather than as policies that could be withdrawn. Those with dollar debt and peso income ran a currency mismatch they did not price. Rule 63 follows.

Question 4. Name the three leaks on a cross-border transfer.

Answer: The exchange spread, the transaction fees including intermediary banks, and the cost of delay, both lost time value and adverse currency movement while money waits.

Question 5. Why might a bank freeze funds without telling you why?

Answer: Because anti-money-laundering law can require it to report a suspicion and forbid it from telling the customer. The freeze may not be about you being guilty; it may be the bank meeting a duty it cannot discuss.

Question 6. What should you never say in a bank onboarding meeting?

Answer: That you want to skip beneficial-owner details, that you could split a deposit, that your other bank did not need this, or asking whether something will be reported.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

REGA mapped the three gates: registration, controls and the bank. Ford and Roman took Argentina 2001 to 2002, where a decade-long peg and access to deposits proved to be policies, giving Rule 63. Nadia counted the spread, the fees and the wait, and showed they fall on equity. Omar laid out the three rulebooks: investment, exchange and anti-money-laundering, with a Canada and Guyana comparison to verify. Roman priced a remittance route and its narrowed-gate case. REGA ran the bank onboarding meeting.

Red Pen

Read this hypothetical internal memo and find the defects before reading on.

Memo: funding the project company. Our co-investor will send 1,500,000 dollars next week through his holding company; he says his bank has already checked it, so we need not ask for ownership details. To save time, our lawyer's assistant will wire our own 1,000,000 dollar contribution from her personal account, and we will register the capital later if needed. The pro forma converts all capital at the screen rate. Profit will be held in the project company until sale and remitted in one payment. We will open the project account at the end of the month.

The defects. First, relying on another bank's checks: our bank must do its own due diligence, and we need the co-investor's beneficial owners and source of funds before money moves. Second, wiring our capital through a third party's personal account breaks the evidence trail and looks exactly like what anti-money-laundering rules are designed to catch. Third, "register later if needed" ignores that registration may be what protects remittance at exit, and may have a deadline. Fourth, converting at the screen rate overstates the money reaching the project. Fifth, holding all profit to a single remittance maximises exposure to a narrowed gate. Sixth, the money arrives next week but the account opens at month end: funds will arrive with nowhere lawful and documented to land.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "Why do we need all this paperwork just to move our own money?" Then compare.

Model answer: "Because money we own abroad is not the same as money we can use. It has to pass three gates. Some countries want foreign capital registered, and that record is what protects our right to take it out later. Exchange rules, or plain shortage of dollars, can limit converting and sending profit, sometimes overnight, as Argentina showed in 2001. And every bank must know who really owns us and where the money came from, or it will hold the payment. So we register where it matters, keep proof of every dollar in, give the bank a complete file before it asks, hold two banks, keep part of our reserve in the currency we spend, and distribute profit as we earn it. The paperwork is cheap. A frozen payment, or profit stuck behind a gate, is not."

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name all three gates? Did you give one concrete control for each? Did you finish inside two minutes? Record it again tomorrow if not.

Kema's study note

If one answer this week came slowly, it is probably the difference between the three rulebooks. Write them on a card: investment rules decide if the state wants your money; exchange rules decide if it can leave; anti-money-laundering rules decide if a bank will carry it. Then attach one control to each: a condition precedent for investment approval, a reserve and distribution policy for exchange, and a standing evidence pack for the bank. Say the card aloud once a day this week. By Friday you should not need it.

One more test of understanding. Take any structure chart you have seen in this phase and ask, for each arrow, which of the three rulebooks applies to it and what evidence moves it. If an arrow has no answer, that is the next question for counsel.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is designing a structure that is tax-efficient and legally sound but cannot move money when it matters. The control is to test every structure against the three gates before you form a single entity.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming that what is legal is also possible. A lawful remittance that no bank will process and no central bank will supply currency for is still stuck.

Callback

In Week 35, Omar and LEX taught that minute books and signing authority are load-bearing. A bank's due diligence reads those same documents. A clean minute book is not housekeeping; it is the evidence that lets your money move.

Recap

Three gates: registration, controls and the bank. Three leaks: spread, fees and time. Three rulebooks: investment, exchange and anti-money-laundering. Rule 63: never let your ability to pay depend on a currency promise or bank access you do not control.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was about whether money can move. Cross-border money passes three gates: registration with the state, which in some countries protects the right to remit capital later; exchange rules or practical scarcity, which decide whether currency can be converted and sent; and a bank willing to carry it under know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering duties. Argentina in 2001 and 2002 showed what happens when a currency peg and access to deposits turn out to be policies: Rule 63, never let my ability to pay depend on a currency promise or bank access I do not control. Every transfer leaks through the spread, the fees and the wait, and those costs fall on equity. So I register where it protects me, keep proof of every dollar in, give my bank a complete ownership and source-of-funds file before it asks, hold two banks, keep reserves in the currency I spend and distribute profit as it is earned.
terms: Flow-of-funds map — a one-page diagram of every entity, bank, currency and approval money passes through, in and out.
Source of funds — the documented origin of the money used in a transaction, such as a property sale or retained earnings.
Remittance — sending money from one country to another, such as profit returned to an investor.

hostile.q: If capital controls arrive the month before your sale closes, how do your investors get paid?
hostile.a: Partly from the dollar reserve held outside the country, which is sized to cover the first distribution. The rest from local currency used to pay remaining local costs, and through the conversion queue at the rationed amount, which my downside case already prices. Investors know that schedule now, before it happens, because it is in their reporting.
